nameStory: The toothed jelly fungus gets its wonderfully descriptive name from its unique combination of features that feel like a nature mashup. Its cap has a jiggly, gelatinous texture like jello, while underneath it sports tiny tooth-like projections instead of regular gills. Some folks call it 'cat's tongue' because those little teeth give it the same rough, bumpy texture as a kitty's tongue!
description: The toothed jelly fungus is one of nature's more unusual creations - imagine a small, translucent mushroom that feels like firm jello when you touch it. These fascinating fungi typically grow 1-4 inches across with whitish to pale brownish caps that are often irregularly shaped, sometimes looking more like rubbery brackets than typical mushrooms. What makes them truly special is their undersurface, covered in soft, tooth-like spines instead of gills, giving them an almost alien appearance. They're one of the few fungi that combine a jelly-like texture with a toothed spore-bearing surface.

idTips.label: Teeth/Spines
idTips.description: Look underneath for soft, white to pale tooth-like projections hanging down like tiny icicles - this is the most distinctive feature and replaces traditional gills

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels rubbery and gelatinous like firm jello - you can squeeze it and it bounces back to shape

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Translucent to semi-transparent, whitish to pale brown, often irregularly shaped and sometimes bracket-like rather than traditionally mushroom-shaped

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: May have a short, lateral stem or be stemless and attached directly to wood - when present, the stem shares the same jelly-like texture

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Very mild, pleasant mushroom odor with no strong or offensive scents

idTips.label: Growing Pattern
idTips.description: Often grows in overlapping clusters or shelving groups on dead wood, especially conifers

habitat: Look for toothed jelly fungi on dead coniferous wood throughout New England's forests, particularly on fallen logs, stumps, and dead branches of pine, fir, and spruce trees. They thrive in moist, shaded woodland areas from sea level to mountain elevations, especially where there's consistent humidity. You'll often find them in mixed or coniferous forests where dead wood stays damp for extended periods.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing on well-rotted logs as temperatures warm and spring rains provide consistent moisture. Look for small, developing specimens that are especially translucent.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when warm temperatures and summer humidity create ideal conditions. Fresh specimens are most abundant and display their characteristic jelly-like texture best.
seasonality.fall: Continue fruiting through autumn, especially during wet periods. Late-season specimens may be found alongside other wood-decomposing fungi on the same logs.
seasonality.winter: Generally dormant, though dried specimens may persist on logs and can rehydrate during warm winter thaws to briefly resume their gelatinous appearance.

funFact: This remarkable fungus can completely dry out during drought conditions, becoming paper-thin and crispy, then magically spring back to its full jelly-like glory within hours of getting wet again - it's like a natural sponge that can resurrect itself!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other jelly fungi like Tremella species (witch's butter), but those lack the distinctive teeth underneath and are usually more irregular in shape. Remember: if it's gelatinous AND has teeth hanging underneath, you've found the toothed jelly fungus - no other local fungus combines these two features.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'edible' in some sources, this fungus is more of a texture curiosity than a culinary delight - it's nearly flavorless and has an unusual rubbery consistency that most people find unappetizing. It's one of the few fungi that demonstrates remarkable desiccation tolerance, making it a fascinating example of biological adaptation.
compareHints: The toothed jelly fungus is actually quite unique in New England - it's the only common fungus that combines a gelatinous texture with tooth-like spines underneath. While other jelly fungi like Tremella mesenterica (witch's butter) share the rubbery texture, they lack teeth entirely and are typically bright yellow. Regular toothed fungi in the Hydnum family have the spines but are firm and fleshy rather than gelatinous, making this species unmistakable once you know what to look for.
